title: Dot products and weighted sums
goals: Calculate a dot product by matching feature positions
Explain how a weight changes a score with other inputs fixed
Distinguish a weighted score from a probability or trained model
vocabulary: A numerical coefficient multiplying one input component
The sum of products of corresponding vector components
The product of one input component and its matching weight
A numerical output whose interpretation must be specified

blocks.title: Multiply matching components then add
blocks.caption: The first two rows are separate contributions. The last row combines them; multiplying the final input sum by the final weight sum would be a different operation.

blocks.label: Keep w = [2, -1]. Change [4, 2] to [4, 3]. Compute both contributions and explain the score change.

guided_practice.title: Explain cancellation
guided_practice.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [2, 4], explain why score zero does not mean the input contains no information.
guided_practice.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions 4 and -4 cancel. The input still contains width 2 and height 4; zero is the combined score.

independent_case.title: Compute a new dot product independently
independent_case.task: Use x = [3, 1, 2] and w = [-2, 4, 0.5]. Give each contribution and the total. Increase only the second component from 1 to 2 and compute the new total. Explain why a two-weight list is invalid for this input.
independent_case.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions -6, 4, 1 give -1. With second component 2, contributions -6, 8, 1 give 3, a rise of 4. Three input components need three matching weights; silently dropping the final component changes the computation.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: The operation is 2 times 4 plus -1 times 2, not (2 - 1) times (4 + 2). That shortcut happens to match for some inputs but is not the rule.
A negative coefficient changes direction. Units, data and the rest of the model affect interpretation.
These values were supplied. Training would require data, an objective and a fitting procedure.

blocks.text: Keep w = [2, -1] fixed. For A = [4, 2], the score is 6. For B = [2, 4], it is 4 - 4 = 0. For C = [3, 3], it is 6 - 3 = 3. Swapping input positions without swapping their matching weights changes the computation. A zero score can come from cancellation, even when neither input is zero.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The length check matters: Python zip alone stops at the shorter list and could silently omit a feature. The function assumes numeric inputs already validated under the schema. First predict the three printed values on paper, then compare.
